job.style: a news-style report about a real-world situation

passage: In a recent experiment, a new AI system was trained to identify medical images by processing thousands of X-ray scans. Unlike simple computer programs that follow a rigid list of pre-written rules, this AI learned by identifying patterns within the data it was shown. However, the system struggled when it encountered images from a different hospital with slightly different lighting. This revealed that an AI is not a universal genius; a system excellent at medical diagnosis cannot automatically drive a car or write poetry. Furthermore, researchers discovered that because the training data mostly featured patients from one specific demographic, the AI became less accurate for other groups. This bias was not caused by a programmer intentionally writing unfair code, but by the limited variety in the data itself. Even when the AI confidently presented its findings in a professional report, some of its conclusions were factually incorrect. This proves that an AI’s output is not guaranteed to be true just because it sounds authoritative or because it has been trained on a large dataset. Users must remember that AI systems are tools that learn from examples, and their performance depends entirely on the quality and diversity of the information they are given.

items.evidence: Unlike simple computer programs that follow a rigid list of pre-written rules, this AI learned by identifying patterns within the data it was shown.
items.q: How did this AI learn to identify medical images?
options: By finding patterns in the X-ray scans it saw
By following a fixed list of pre-written rules
Programmers typed in the answer for every scan
By working it out without seeing any scans
items.explain: Unlike simple rule-following programs, this AI learned by spotting patterns in the X-ray scans it was shown.

wrong.why: thinks AI is just any rule-following computer program
thinks programmers type in every answer beforehand
thinks an AI can learn without being shown examples

items.evidence: However, the system struggled when it encountered images from a different hospital with slightly different lighting.
items.q: The AI is shown X-rays from another hospital where the lighting is slightly changed. What happens?
options: It struggles, because they are unlike its training scans
It stays correct, because it is already fully trained
It does better, because it has seen thousands of scans
It works the same, because programmers typed in every answer
items.explain: The AI struggled with images from a different hospital because they did not look like the scans it learned from.

wrong.why: thinks a trained AI is always correct on new inputs
thinks many examples of one kind make it good at everything
thinks answers are pre-typed, so inputs do not matter

items.evidence: This revealed that an AI is not a universal genius; a system excellent at medical diagnosis cannot automatically drive a car or write poetry.
items.q: A hospital wants this X-ray AI to also drive its ambulance. What does the passage suggest?
options: It cannot, since its skill is only medical scans
It can, since it is excellent at diagnosis
It can, once it is fitted into a human-like robot
It can, if programmers type in every road rule
items.explain: An AI is not a universal genius; one that is excellent at diagnosis cannot automatically drive a car.

wrong.why: thinks being great at one task means great at all
thinks AI means a human-like robot
thinks programmers just type in all the answers

items.evidence: This bias was not caused by a programmer intentionally writing unfair code, but by the limited variety in the data itself.
items.q: Why did the AI become less accurate for patients from some groups?
options: Its training scans came mostly from one group
A programmer wrote unfair code on purpose
The doctors were unfair, since computers have no opinions
The lighting at the other hospital was different
items.explain: The bias came from limited variety in the data, mostly one group of patients, not from a programmer's unfair code.

wrong.why: thinks bias only comes from a programmer meaning to be unfair
thinks AI cannot be unfair, so blames people
picks a nearby problem from the passage that is not the cause

items.evidence: Even when the AI confidently presented its findings in a professional report, some of its conclusions were factually incorrect.
items.q: The AI produces a neat, confident report. What should a doctor think about it?
options: It needs checking, as some of its findings were false
It needs no checking, as it sounds so sure
It needs no checking, as it trained on many scans
It needs no checking if another AI agrees
items.explain: Even confident, professional reports from the AI had some factually incorrect conclusions, so its output must be checked.

wrong.why: thinks a sure, neat answer must be correct
thinks a well-trained AI is always right
thinks two AIs agreeing proves the answer is correct
